newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom debuts amid buying fever.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom debuts amid buying fever.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG stock took off in a buying frenzy Monday in Europe's biggest stock offering and the second biggest in history.
The stock market exploded in a frenzy of activity, with more than 38 million shares changing hands -- marking a revolution for Germans, who have traditionally been wary of investing in stocks.
The initial public offering, worth up to 20 billion marks ($13 billion), is second in the world only to the 1987 listing of Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp.

After initial indications that shares in Europe's biggest telecommunications company would trade in a range of 31 to 34 marks (about $21 to $23), the stock exchange quoted the first official price in midsession at 33.20 marks ($22.04) and they closed at 33.90 ($22.50).
On the New York Stock Exchange, Deutsche Telekom's stock added $2.73 to $21.625 in extremely heavy trading, making it the most heavily traded issue on the Big Board by early afternoon.

About 100 traders rushed market makers to place orders and shouted in unison "33.20! 33.20!" as Telekom Chairman Ron Sommer and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel waded into the crowd with broad smiles on their faces.

The chief executives of Germany's leading banks -- Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG -- who had coordinated the global listing, stood on stairs overlooking the trading floor evidently pleased as new life seemed to pour into Germany's stock market.
"This moment is a milestone in the development of the market," said Werner Seifert, chairman of Deutsche Boerse AG, umbrella group for Germany's eight regional stock exchanges.
"This is a decisive contribution to strengthening the equity culture among private investors in Germany."
The road to Frankfurt, Germany's main stock market, was a long one for Deutsche Telekom.
In 1989, the government split it off from the postal authority and in 1995 it became a stock company owned by the state.
After the issue of 713 million shares, the public now owns 26 percent of Telekom, which has annual sales of 66 billion marks ($43.8 billion).

Marking a watershed in German investment culture, nearly 2 million ordinary Germans shed fears of "risky" stock investments and cracked open their piggy banks to buy Telekom stock, making up just under half of the total offering.

Shares were also snatched up at the 28.50-mark ($18.92) issue price by institutional investors worldwide -- which stock market and government officials said should pave the way for other German companies to make such global share offerings.
"The privatisation of Deutsche Telekom, with decisive stimulus for financial markets, is tied to the popularisation of shareholdings," Finance Minister Waigel said.
Deutsche Telekom itself painted the town pink, putting its corporate colour on chandeliers, baseball caps handed out to passersby and even the walls of the stock exchange.
Dealers said trade in Telekom shares dominated Monday's session, but they were divided over how high the shares could climb.
One trader said it appeared as though private stockholders were already beginning to take profits.
